items.title: San Francisco's best hotel cannot be killed
items.content:
I am not a rock star, although I like to imagine myself as one. I imagine it so, so hard: packed stadiums, crowds numbering five figures going wild as I take my shirt off, shady managers hanging out backstage ready to ply me with Hefty bags full of pharmaceutical cocaine. But it’s too late for me, on the cusp of 50, to actually become a rock star — it certainly couldn’t be a skill or charisma issue, no sir — which is why there’s a tiny slice of the hospitality industry that exists to make patrons like me FEEL like rock stars, if only for a brief moment. 

This is where the legendary Phoenix Hotel, plopped down on Eddy Street right in the middle of San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, comes in.

I have stayed at many hotels in San Francisco, but all of them were hotels. Elevator banks. Free continental breakfast. A sad gym on the third floor where one treadmill is always busted. You know the kind of hotel I mean. The Phoenix, which opened in the 1980s at the influence of legendary rock promoter Bill Graham, is not that kind of hotel. This was a place dreamed up to serve real-deal rock stars, and to make anyone else staying there feel like part of the greater entourage.

Article continues below this ad

And until early this year, it was all set to die young, as so many of its more famous guests had, Kurt Cobain chief among them. Late in 2025, b. Patisserie co-owner Michel Suas was readying to take over the Phoenix’s lot and close down the hotel permanently, presumably using the land to build some kind of overpriced but good boulangerie. But at the last second, Suas had a change of heart! HONH HONH HONH! Enter local hotelier Binoy Patel, who took the reins of the property and is keeping the hotel open. That’s right, like a phoenix rising from the ashes. You read my mind to the letter.

Given this fortuitous stay of execution, my SFGATE bosses thought that I should stay at the Phoenix during my annual “Drew comes to the Bay Area for a weekand eatsway too much” trip two months ago. As a Marylander, I was ignorant to the Phoenix’s charms before booking my room. It is now my favorite hotel in the city, and if new owner Patel messes with so much as a single AC outlet in the place, he and I will have words.

I didn’t expect to love the Phoenix as much as I did, certainly not at first glance. No one stays in the Tenderloin for the Tenderloin. You stay in this part of town because you have some work engagement nearby. That’s why hotelier Chip Conley founded the hotel in the first place; it was close to venues where Graham booked gigs for headline acts. Otherwise, the place is located on a nondescript, run-down stretch of Eddy Street that’s a relative desert. The hotel itself is a refurbished roadside motel, the kind of place I’d normally expect to be murdered in. The only thing shielding your room door from the rest of the world is a red iron gate to the street next to the hotel office. So my first thought before ringing the front office door was, “This place better not suck.”

Article continues below this ad

I was buzzed by a clerk who bore more than passing resemblance to Sweetums the Muppet: a bulky, tatted-up fellow with long scraggy hair and the beard to match. Sweetums could have been the bouncer at a Hells Angels bar if he wasn’t such a sweetheart. Instead, he manned the front desk at the Phoenix and warmly offered me a number of vital pointers. I needed to use my key card at the red gate anytime I came or went, there was always free coffee in the front office if I needed it, and logging onto the hotel’s Wi-Fi required him to perform a live demo for me.

“I can’t do it the usual way?” I asked Sweetums.

“Doing it the usual way here is s—t,” he told me. But doing it his way worked like a charm.

Article continues below this ad

I walked into a concrete courtyard loosely festooned with palm trees, potted succulents, and basket chairs surrounding a fat round pool. An outdoor performance stage loomed toward the back. No one was swimming in the pool when I first entered the courtyard; the water was populated exclusively by aging pool noodles, some of which had bite marks in them. But the water looked clean, which is more than you can say for the average Motel 6 pool. I crossed the courtyard to the outdoor staircase leading up to my second floor room. Standing sentry by the staircase was a huge, colorfully tiled sculpture of a frog playing the guitar. Your mother would describe this hotel as “kind of funky,” and she’d be correct.

But the ultimate test for this kind of novelty hotel is your room itself. You want a hotel that’s only seedy. I’ve stayed at actual seedy hotels … the kind of hotels where s—t doesn’t work. They are not charming. So my room at the Phoenix would determine which side of the line the hotel fell on.

Article continues below this ad

If you’ve read this far, you won’t be surprised to learn that my room was perfect. One side of it was dominated by a floor-to-ceiling window looking out onto the courtyard, just in case any other guests wanted to watch me and a groupie going at it. Seeing as how I’ve been faithfully married for 24 years, the chances of me indulging in that particular rock star fantasy were minimal. But it was nice to know I had the option if I so chose.

As for the room itself, it had everything I would have wanted from a mainstream hotel room. The bed was comfy. There were multiple charging outlets available to me, many hidden inside of retro furnishings that scanned like film props. And I didn’t need a tutorial from Sweetums on how to operate the shower or the light switches. My only beef was that the soft neon lamp hanging over my bed didn’t work, but I probably wouldn’t have used it for longer than two minutes anyway.

This was a goodass hotel room, and it served as a perfect base of operations for me as I spent all week covering assignments in North Beach, Cow Hollow, Marin, Palo Alto, and elsewhere. Anytime I was slogging through my day of field reporting, I knew that my plush room at the Phoenix would be waiting for me. Best of all, when I asked Sweetums if there were any good places for breakfast nearby, he immediately told me to hit Brenda’s French Soul Food, another local institution I had been heretofore unaware of. I went to Brenda’s the following morning and ordered the bananas foster French toast, plus a breakfast sandwich. You know, for balance. I ate so well that brunch, I needed to burn some serious calories afterward.

Article continues below this ad

And where better to do that than in the Phoenix pool?

This was August, mind you. Temperatures in San Francisco that time of year aren’t always conducive to pool days, so I suited up with the mercury hovering around a crisp 65 in the hotel’s courtyard. I fully expected the water to be even colder than that, so imagine my surprise when I jumped off the edge and KERSPLOOSH! Suddenly I was warmer and happier than I’d been all trip. The Phoenix pool isn’t so hot as to feel gross, it’s just well calibrated for a warm swim in a city that wants you to slowly freeze to death. Once in the pool, I knew immediately that leaving the pool would render me a pile of chattering teeth. So I grabbed one of the chewed-up pool noodles and lounged to my big fat heart’s content.

Article continues below this ad

I felt no danger from the dirty street outside, nor did I feel embarrassed to be a 49-year-old man, rash guard and all, swimming all by himself in the middle of a random weekday. I know that Sweetums was standing sentry at the front desk, and I knew that I was exactly where I wanted to be: kicking back in the heart of one of the best cities in the world, with not a single worry on my mind. If that’s not the life of a rock star, I don’t know what is.

items.title: Steven Spielberg's new film is his best in decades
items.content:
I put a question to my SFGATE colleagues just the other day that had them mulling for a bit: What’s the last great movie that Steven Spielberg directed? I’m not talking about a merely film. The old man can put together a competent picture anytime he likes. I’m talking about an all-timer of a Spielberg movie, something that belongs up there with his best work, which includes “Jaws,” “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” “E.T.,” “Schindler’s List” and … you get the idea. When you’re a director who’s made not just one of the greatest movies of all time but of them, audience members like me hope for (and oftentimes ) greatness from you with every subsequent project. Such is the standard that Spielberg, father of the modern blockbuster, set for himself. It’s also a standard that, in my opinion, he has not reached since the release of “Catch Me If You Can,” his note-perfect caper film, back in 2002. The bulk of my colleagues agreed, which led to a much more pointed question: Is Steven Spielberg washed?

With the release this week of his latest movie, “Disclosure Day,” I can now tell you, the reader, that the answer is no. Steven Spielberg, much to my relief, is still very much Steven Spielberg. This is the best film he’s made in nearly a quarter century. I have no idea if it’ll ascend to the status of an enduring classic — only time gets to decide that—but goddamn, what a movie.

If you’re unfamiliar with the premise of “Disclosure Day,” perhaps because it has a clunky title that reminds viewers like me of that one time Demi Moore sexually harassed Michael Douglas, I can get you situated real quick (and relatively spoiler-free). Steven Spielberg has made another movie about extraterrestrials. That’s really all you need to know, isn’t it? You know that Spielberg is in his element when he’s spinning a yarn about little green men from outer space. It’s a subject that aligns perfectly with his directorial sensibilities: the wonder of the unknown, the idea that we are not alone, kids who have serious daddy issues, things of that nature. So long as you’re not watching “Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull,” you know that your alien story is in good hands with this man.

Article continues below this ad

This time around, our story is about Daniel Kellner (rising star Josh O’Connor), a pencil-pusher at a shadowy defense corporation who opens the film having stolen a precious MacGuffin, among other things, from his boss Noah Scanlon (Colin Firth). You know what big meanies the men in suits are in a Spielberg flick. Firth, operating at peak Colin Firth, plays his character no different. Scanlon wants his MacGuffin back and sends out a legion of underlings in black cars to capture Kellner and blow stuff up real good.

Meanwhile, a flighty weatherlady in Kansas City named Margaret Fairchild (Emily Blunt, flawless) sees a red cardinal fly into her apartment one day, and suddenly, she can read minds, speak fluent Korean and involuntarily break out into alien clucks in the middle of a live broadcast. Blunt’s weatherlady gets visions of O’Connor’s Kellner in her head and feels the urgent need to go to him despite having no idea where he is. At the same time, Kellner has to get the extraterrestrial artifact he stole from the bad men in suits to the only good one he knows (Oscar nominee Colman Domingo), who appears to be hiding out inside a studio soundstage somewhere in the Midwest. There’s also a lapsed nun played by Bono’s daughter.

Article continues below this ad

By now, you’re already asking me, “Hey man, where are the goddamn aliens in all this?” Well, turns out that Firth’s bad guy has been overseeing a government plot to not only suppress evidence of close encounters of the third kind here on Earth but also video footage of the U.S. government doing unspeakable things to those aliens and exploiting their extraterrestrial resources for questionable purposes. Pick the allegory of your choice from that morsel. O’Connor not only wants the government to pay for his atrocities but also wants to “disclose,” on a single “day,” all of these secrets to the world at large.

This is where the Spielberg difference is most prevalent. Any movie can stage a 2.5-hour chase for some ET microfiche, but Spielberg (credited here with the screen story) uses the concept of a disclosure day to ask deeper questions. Can humankind handle this knowledge? Will people accept the existence of aliens, especially in a time of deepfakes?  they accept it, especially if the aliens in question are a superior life-form? Could humans adopt this life-form as their new god and throw out all of the old religions? Spielberg makes time, all throughout “Disclosure Day,” to hammer away at these unanswerable questions. He also makes sure to throw in a brilliant comic sequence about how hard it is to run over your own cellphone with a sedan. All of that detail gives the action sequences much higher stakes than a cookie-cutter tentpole movie would. 

Article continues below this ad

And those action sequences kick ass, especially a brilliant train crash sequence that perfectly echoes a toy train crash sequence from his movie, the autobiographical “The Fabelmans.” I didn’t pee once during “Disclosure Day.” Didn’t even think about doing it. I was way too invested in what was going to happen to all of the characters in it, and to humanity as a result. A lot of summer blockbusters tell you that the fate of humankind hangs in the balance. Here’s a movie that actually shows you that view from the precipice. So when we finally reach the movie’s climax, you, the viewer, are just as riveted by what’s unfolding as the characters are.

This isn’t a perfect movie. Spielberg holds off on his cornier instincts for the bulk of “Disclosure Day” but eventually dips into the simple syrup. Firth misses his dead wife. O’Connor and Blunt miss their respective lost childhoods. A kiddie actor encounters a bunch of friendly CGI animals (my daughter said they looked like AI) and then walks into a super bright light. That, too, you expect from a Spielberg picture. After all, “Jaws” was the last utterly unsentimental movie he made, and that was half a century ago. But for “Disclosure Day,” Spielberg reins in those impulses as best he can and delivers not only one of the best movies of the summer but the best film that he himself has made in decades. The old man’s still got it, and we’re lucky to have him.

items.title: Congratulations, the Reflecting Pool is now a swamp
items.content:
The one thing that Washington, D.C., has always had going for it is its beauty. The people who run America from this town have always been an unsightly bunch, but they’ve done their nasty work in a city that has acquired, over the course of this country’s lifespan, an aesthetic like no other. No other major American city looks as regally beautiful as D.C. You and I have a long-standing federal law to thank for this, but we also have a collection of national landmarks clustered in the center of the district that the aforementioned law was written to both protect and to showcase. The Capitol. The Lincoln Memorial. The Washington Monument. These are gorgeous edifices, ones designed to outlast old generations and to inspire newer ones. They are the best of D.C., and therefore the best of America.

Not content to let an army of UFC slobs desecrate the capital this past weekend, nor to personally oversee the physical ruination of the White House earlier this year, Trump has now decided to destroy the humble Reflecting Pool along the National Mall. You’ve probably heard about the Reflecting Pool situation: how President Cronyism dished out a no-bid contract to renovate the pool earlier this spring to a company that had done work at his Virginia golf club, how the project came in over budget (big surprise), and how the results have turned out disastrously, with algae blooms overtaking the pool within moments of its unveiling. 

Article continues below this ad

Because I’m a rubbernecker by nature, on Tuesday I decided to head down to the National Mall to see the damage myself. Come with me now on a quick trip to a national treasure that has now become the world’s dullest aquarium.

Article continues below this ad

It’s a gorgeous day to visit the mall. The weather outside is flawless and, because it’s a Tuesday, tourist traffic is at a relative minimum. Normally, this would be an ideal day to sit by the Reflecting Pool and meditate on freedom, democracy and other quaint notions. But the second I make my way into the heart of the mall, between the Lincoln Memorial and the World War II Memorial, I see an expanse of wet, sickly green. Like the ocean on a bad day. I have never seen the Reflecting Pool look this ugly. Trump’s goal with this renovation was to paint the bottom of the pool “American flag blue,” an idiotic idea because this pool is specifically not supposed to be ANY color. Previous administrations have kept the water here clean and clear so that it can, you know, reflect, so that visitors could look into the pool’s waters and see in it the royal blue sky, the wedding cake white clouds, the stately gray monument on the hill next door. You’re not supposed to look into this pool and see anything but the surrounding splendor, your pretty little face included.

When I look into the pool now, I see nothing but green murk. The algae is still here, and it’s still defeating Trump’s cleanup crews handily. One of those crews is working a corner of the pool near the Lincoln Memorial. They’re all National Park Service staffers, overseen by Trump’s metaphorical pool boy Doug Burgum. One of them orders the others, “Let’s get this hose in the water and be sure not to twist it.” The hose is attached to a small, roving pool vacuum. It’s not a fair fight, unkinked hose or no. Just a few weeks ago, Trump was bragging that this pool was “bigger than skyscrapers.” He even made a definitely scientifically accurate chart to prove the point. Turns out that hugeness can really bite you in the ass when your very large and strong pool has an infestation problem.

Article continues below this ad

I walk along the esplanade, and more Park Service crews mar the view. I see a couple more vacuums. Even uglier, I see a number of hoses languishing in the pool, looking like the tentacles of some evil monster and spewing a white foam into the depths. These machines are presumably the “nanobubblers” that the Park Service, perhaps now helmed by Russell Wilson, claims have “successfully destroyed the algae bloom.” They have not. All they appear to be doing is troubling the water enough so that it has an even less reflective quality. I’d have better odds seeing my reflection in a cinder block.

I kneel by the pool and dip my hand into the water. Thankfully, my flesh doesn’t instantly dissolve upon contact with it. I feel along the inside of the pool, and it’s slimy to the touch. Six years ago, I bought our family an inflatable hot tub to stave off boredom during the COVID-19 pandemic, another Trump production. I didn’t know anything about pool maintenance, so the water in that hot tub also turned green, and the insides of it were slimy in the exact same way the pool’s insides are right now. I can be forgiven for my negligence back then, because I was a bored rookie. When you’re the richest nation in world history, you don’t deserve quite as much slack.

Article continues below this ad

I take my hand out of the water and lick my fingers. The water tastes fine. If I end up hospitalized with diphtheria later tonight, my editors will update this post accordingly.

I continue walking the esplanade, and the water only gets dirtier. In one corner, the pool looks like it’s been the victim of a gasoline spill. There’s a lone duckling swimming around in this failed Jackson Pollock work, and I desperately want to fish it out with a net and help it find its mommy.

Then I look over to the nearby World War II Memorial. Opened in 2004, this memorial features a fountain pool at its center, flanked by 50 pillars representing fallen combat veterans from every state. And wouldn’t you know it, the fountain pool is pristine. We’re literally feet away from the befouled Reflecting Pool, and the difference is staggering. I can see reflections in this other pool! Some of them blue! I see tourists happily dipping their bare feet into its waters! I see an American landmark that looks the way it’s supposed to look, the way these landmarks always looked until Trump and his power frown came along to destroy it all.

Article continues below this ad

I walk back to my car. Along the way I cross through the Constitution Gardens, which boasts its own serene pond. The water in this pond is dirtier than the WWII monument’s water, but it’s still unscathed by the algae blooms. I edge closer to the pond and see a family of ducks, little baby ducklings included, frolicking happily in the water. These ducks are smart. They know the good stuff when they see it. Maybe we should let them run this city.

items.title: Brandon Aiyuk's NFL career is already over
items.content:
The NFL has had itself one miserable offseason. You may have been too busy watching America self-immolating to notice, but the football men have been behaving incredibly badly of late. Falcons edge rusher James Pearce got arrested for allegedly being a psycho boyfriend to Chicago Sky forward Rickea Jackson. The Denver Broncos have a sudden, and grotesque, DV problem on their hands. Terrion Arnold just got dropped by the Lions after being arrested on suspicion of kidnapping. And New England coach Mike Vrabel can’t seem to keep his little Pat Patriot in his trousers. All of it either has been ugly or has served as a portent of more ugliness to come. 

Which brings us to the curious story of 49ers wideout Brandon Aiyuk, whose recent behavior has gone from maddening to outright frightening. Just two years ago, Aiyuk re-upped with the team after posting a career-high 1,342 receiving yards, making All-Pro and helping the Niners reach the Super Bowl the season prior. Wideouts tend to be mercurial in nature, but they also represent one of the highest-value non-QB positions in the NFL, right up there alongside left tackles and edge rushers. So when the Niners braintrust gave Aiyuk his money after the usual contentious negotiation phase, no one could really blame it. Paying Aiyuk ensured that he, alongside QB Brock Purdy, would keep the team in contention through the rest of the decade. Two years later … 

The above video represents perhaps the world’s saddest attempt at making it rain. It’s also just one in a series of Insta posts from Aiyuk that, taken in aggregate, are more distressing than they are laughable. Aiyuk played only half a season after his contract extension, tearing his knee up midway through the 2024 campaign and then ghosting on the team entirely in 2025. Throughout all of this, Aiyuk has been posting videos of himself driving at Jose Canseco speeds, calling the Niners stupid, demanding the team cut him so that he can sign with the Washington Commanders (no word on if the Commanders are actually open to the prospect, and signs are pointing to the contrary), and finally threatening to whip the entire organization with a belt:  

Article continues below this ad

“They running from that belt that’s on the way. It’s inevitable. It’s coming. Stop running.” 

Normally I’d consider the “belt” in a quote like this to be metaphorical. But in this case, I cannot discount the possibility that yes, Brandon Aiyuk would like to physically remove his belt and assault Niners personnel with it. Because his behavior over the past two years has gone well beyond the usual “the enemy speaks kindly & holds a knife” genre of posting that you and I usually get from our nation’s disgruntled wideout population. Aiyuk has openly taunted Bay Area law enforcement to come arrest him, fired his agent for being too cozy with Niners GM John Lynch, posted cryptic pleas to the NFLPA for being too cozy with that agent, and accused Lynch of showing up at his house unannounced, stalker-style. I am not a doctor, but I’ve been around long enough to recognize when someone is behaving in a deeply unwell manner online. Donald Trump is unwell online. These AI evangelists are unwell online. And Brandon Aiyuk is unwell online. 

In most circumstances, NFL teams have been willing to overlook this kind of s—t. Hell, your own Niners gainfully employed Terrell Owens for many years, despite the fact that TO was a galactic asswipe (who made homophobic comments to boot). In fact, the NFL serves as perhaps our most visible example of what Americans say they won’t tolerate versus what they  won’t tolerate. There isn’t a set of hard criteria for this, of course. If there were, our Supreme Court would already be a pile of ashes by now. Oh, to dream. 

Article continues below this ad

But it’s telling that Aiyuk’s behavior has rendered him radioactive across the league at the same time that Terrion Arnold’s legal trouble proved too much for the Lions to withstand, and that erstwhile Texas Tech QB Brendan Sorsby was denied entry in the NFL’s supplemental draft after he was outed as a severe gambling addict. The league will only let you hang around if you’re either too expensive to get rid of (Deshaun Watson) or not worth the trouble at any price. Given that San Francisco has already partially voided Aiyuk’s deal, and given that no other franchise has expressed any interest in taking him on, the wideout has clearly fallen into the latter category. If there were any sign that his mental state was improving, he’d be on another team’s roster right now. 

He’s not, and it’s fair to speculate that his behavior — what’s been made public about it and what’s probably been going around the league’s sprawling gossip network about it — has been so alarming that no one in the NFL dare preside over his further descent into madness. And I mean ever. Not this coming season, and not in any season to come. The man’s career is over. This is tragic from a mercenary perspective; the guy could ball when he was inclined to. But it now feels tragic in a much more general sense. I can’t tell you what exactly is wrong with Brandon Aiyuk. But I can tell you that if the NFL wants nothing to do with him, it’s worse than any of us can probably imagine.

items.title: It's easy to blame the USMNT's World Cup crashout on one man. So I will.
items.content:
Much like our nation itself, the World Cup run for the U.S. men’s national soccer team started off promisingly, only to become a sick joke. The USMNT got eliminated from the 2026 Cup on Monday night after Belgium crushed it 4-1, in a game where the home team was thoroughly outplayed, outclassed and outcoached. But if the loss itself stung, the context in which it was played only made it feel that much worse.  

Yes, that backstory includes Donald Trump, but to a small degree, it also involves USMNT poster child and possible Trump fanboy Christian Pulisic. The first man disgraced the team off the field. The second man disgraced the team on it. How did all of this come to pass? Well, I suppose it’s my job to explain it, although the prospect of doing so excites about as much as having my legs ripped clean off my body. 

This year’s USMNT was, by a few tangible measures, better than any other in recent memory. The U.S. won its group for only the third time in team history. It won two games in group play, which the USMNT had never done before, and by an aggregate score of 6-1. In fact, only three teams scored more goals than the USMNT in group play this tournament. Most important, the Americans LOOKED like they belonged. I’ve usually had to cheer for U.S. men’s teams that only had a spare handful of players who could cut it as pros abroad. Those teams would inevitably get bounced out of the elimination stages, if not much earlier, by one of the real soccer countries. 

Article continues below this ad

But in group play, this USMNT featured players who had international pro cred, including Pulisic (currently with AC Milan), Malik Tillman (Bayer Leverkusen), Weston McKennie (Juventus), Alex Freeman (Villarreal) and Folarin Balogun (Monaco). This felt like a real team and, for a couple of thrilling weeks, played like it. This USMNT was attacking like the big-boy countries, moving the ball around with precision in the opponent’s goal area and scoring on some truly bitchin’ free kick strikes. If you tried hard, and many fans did, you could picture this USMNT outfit not only hanging with the likes of Belgium but even beating it. 

Balogun, in particular, was one of the players who made that daydream feel so real. But he became infamous in the knockout stage when the refs gave him a late red card for fouling Bosnian midfielder Tarik Muharemovic, which got him ejected from that game and, in theory, from Monday night’s round-of-16 clash with Belgium. You can argue the refs screwed Balo, and the USMNT by extension, with this red card. But fouls in soccer are, as they are in any other sport, partially subjective. Sometimes a foul call goes your way; sometimes it doesn’t. More important, those calls are almost always final. You got hosed by the refs, but whatever. You shake it off and move on. 

As you may have heard, that didn’t happen here. Prior to the Belgium game, FIFA — the wildly corrupt governing body that runs the World Cup — ruled Balogun eligible to play in the match after all. FIFA apparently had its reasons for the reversal, if you care to parse the bureaucratic word salad that it gave for an explanation. But the real reason Balo got to play Monday night was because someone called someone else. That someone? You guessed it. Now join me in audibly groaning for 10 straight minutes: 

The usual outrage ensued. Trump, who had almost certainly never heard of Balogun until a week ago, was outraged that his new favorite athlete was treated very unfairly. Trump’s minions were also outraged by the call. I myself was personally outraged that one of those minions was Rudy Giuliani’s asshole kid. The Bosnians were outraged that Trump got Balo’s suspension lifted. The Belgians were even more outraged by the reversal. The French were outraged that one of their star players received a yellow card. And the Swiss were outraged too, even though no one gives a crap what Switzerland thinks about anything. All of that poisoned the buildup to Monday night’s game so thoroughly that it threatened to tarnish the result, no matter who won.  

Article continues below this ad

But you and I know that sports have always had the ability to transcend their surrounding circumstances. This was already a horribly corrupt World Cup, but matches like England-Mexico and Argentina-Cape Verde redeemed its existence, as these games so often do. So there was a very good chance that Monday night’s tilt between the U.S. and Belgium would, one way or the other, do likewise. After all, Balo was just one player. The USMNT had plenty more where he came from, with Pulisic foremost among them. Pulisic came to this team as a teenage wunderkind and, unlike Freddy Adu, realized his potential with a fruitful career playing abroad. You could argue that the ascendance of Pulisic is the reason why this USMNT had Balo — and McKennie, and Tillman, and Freeman, and the others — on its roster to begin with. Pulisic wasn’t just a great player but a living indicator of just how far U.S. soccer has come this century. That’s why he’s been in every ad during this tournament. He is the face of U.S. Soccer. Our star. Balo or not, we still would’ve had Pulisic at our disposal Monday night, and he still had the ability to deliver a performance that would place him alongside the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Harry Kane, Mo Salah and the rest of soccer royalty.  

Those numbers aren’t an anomaly. Pulisic posted a grand total of zero goals and one assist to his stat line for this entire tournament. He also got hurt more than once. hurt, not pretend hurt just so that he could get some other team’s player red-carded. The USMNT made it this far despite this jackass, not because of him. I spent every USMNT game waiting for this man to do something cool with the ball, and then focusing my attention on players like Balogun instead. And not because Balogun was newer than Pulisic but because he was better. 

Article continues below this ad

You and I should have heeded the warning signs. Pulisic couldn’t help the U.S. get past the knockout stage in the 2022 Cup and couldn’t even help the team qualify for the 2018 edition. He also routinely gets hurt for his European teams, and he has never performed at the levels of this sport’s biggest names, all of whom have proved decisive throughout this World Cup. Worst of all, Pulisic earnestly busted out the Trump dance after scoring a goal one time. I should have known this dickhead was a fraud. I should have known that he’s spent the past few years begging karma to pay him, and his hapless teammates, a visit. Last night, it finally did. 

So I can’t blame Donald Trump alone for this historic embarrassment. I have to blame the team responsible for the loss, and the captain of that team in particular. Ball don’t lie. Christian Pulisic stinks.
