items.title: Andrew Luck is just another bureaucrat now
items.content:
ome with me now to Palo Alto. We’re hopping in the car to make the more than 30-mile drive south of San Francisco to the bucolic campus of Stanford University, where former NFL star Andrew Luck awaits us. The Stanford campus remains as gorgeous, and sheltered, as ever. This is the ideal setting for gifted minds to construct their own realities, and Luck remains one of the more gifted minds that the sport of football has ever produced. Smart enough to read the most complicated defenses at a glance, and smart enough to leave the NFL when he realized that the life of a pro quarterback was making both him, and his wife Nicole, miserable. You could argue that Andrew Luck was too smart for the NFL. But is he smart enough to turn Stanford football into a national powerhouse? That’s what I’m here to find out.

After suddenly retiring from the Indianapolis Colts right before the 2019 season — a decision that the Colts franchise has yet to fully recover from — Luck relocated here to Palo Alto to raise a family amongst the smartypants elite of NorCal. Luck’s first order of business at Stanford, his alma mater, was to re-enroll as a grad student and earn a master’s degree. While doing that, Luck also made a soft reentry into football as a part-time volunteer coach at nearby Palo Alto High School. Finally, in 2024, he made a full reconciliation with the sport by accepting the general manager job of Stanford’s football program.

As administrative gigs go, it’s not an easy one. Luck has taken over a program that hasn’t had a winning record in a full season since 2018, went crawling to the ACC in the wake of the Pac-12’s dissolution three years ago, and is still recovering from the scandalous tenure of former head coach Troy Taylor, a documented chauvinist whom Luck had to fire less than six months into his new job. The general manager position is a relatively new one in college football, one still being defined as the sport stumbles awkwardly into its new semipro incarnation. So, in a relatively short amount of time, Luck has had to hire a new coaching staff, recruit better players and, on top of all that, figure out just what the hell his job here at Stanford is supposed to be.

Article continues below this ad

But if all of that work is stressing Luck out, it doesn’t show on this particular morning. I meet Luck at the university’s Arrillaga Family Sports Center, which serves as both a museum for tourists/recruits and the home of Stanford’s athletic department. You can gawk at all of the memorabilia and life-size images of Stanford sporting greats (Tiger Woods, Bill Walsh, Katie Ledecky, John Elway, Luck himself) that adorn the main floor before you walk upstairs to the football team’s offices, where Luck’s office is situated.

He’s leaner than he was back in his playing days but still has the frame of a world-class athlete, including arms the size of legs. Luck’s work involves pinballing from football offices out to the practice field to consult with his new head coach (and former Stanford teammate) Tavita Pritchard, out on the recruiting trail, and back to the offices again. But Luck doesn’t come off as harried when I meet him. He seems more eager than anything. This is because Andrew Luck loves Stanford, and certainly appears to relish the chance to make its football program — which has sucked for a decade — more than just an occasional player on the national stage.

This too, won’t be easy. The Cardinal is coming off of a 4-8 season under interim head coach Frank Reich, who served as Luck’s head coach in Indy during the QB’s final NFL season. Luck replaced Reich on a permanent basis with Pritchard, whose only coaching experience outside of Palo Alto was a two-year stint as QB coach for the Washington Commanders. Pritchard’s coaching tenure will open successfully a few weeks from now, with a 37-27 win over a middling Hawaii program in Week Zero. But the real opener comes in a matchup with the Miami Hurricanes, a team that made the national final last season, on Friday. That will be the game that shows the nation how far Stanford football has to go, and perhaps give us an idea whether Luck and Pritchard are the men who can lead them there.

Article continues below this ad

But for now it’s still the preseason, so those stakes remain a friendly distance away. Luck leads me into his office so that we can talk about the job in front of him. I don’t get the introspective Luck that was on full display in the near aftermath of his retirement. The Andrew Luck talking to me today is in pitch mode: a bureaucrat here to sell me on his vision for a Stanford football team that has never been to the College Football Playoff and hasn’t won a conference title since 2015.

This Andrew Luck has the requisite glasses/salt-and-pepper beard combination of a university administrator, and he liberally peppers his answers with the word “amazing,” as if saying it over and over will make everything so. Luck tells me he’s much more outgoing than he used to be, although his newfound extraversion doesn’t present as all that natural when we speak. It feels more like prescription socializing than anything else. But I’ll leave you, the reader, to decide that for yourself.

The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: How are you doing?

SFGATE: What would you say is your job here?

It’s a bit amorphous. A lot of fundraising, a lot of recruiting, a lot of bridge-building, both on-campus and out in the community. A lot of getting people to coalesce around an idea that we can be a highly competitive team, and in turn, even competing for conference championships.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: What do you mean by highly competitive? Conference championships?

Absolutely. You get to the playoffs, you have a chance.

SFGATE: Is your end goal consistent contention for national championships?

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Do you think that’s realistic?

Yes, why not? One, this is an amazing institution. You can recruit pretty amazing people here. It’s not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but it amazing. The combination of championship people, coaches and players, the championship process … we have the chance to be a fairly unique program. Retaining and getting talent will be a big part of this job, probably the biggest piece.

SFGATE: Have you had to go out on the recruiting trail yourself?

Article continues below this ad

Not have to. I to. The way the rules have changed in college, they’ve allowed more staff members to go on the road than previously, so it does make sense for me to go out at times.

SFGATE: Does Stanford have a specific radius for recruiting?

No, we recruit nationally. We’re very unique in that we probably only have five or six players that could drive home in less than three hours from here. Coaches have both regions and go everywhere for their position group. I’ve been in the state of Texas to recruit. I’ve been in the state of Washington to recruit. I’ve been in California to recruit.

SFGATE: Is that because of Stanford’s academic and national reputation?

Article continues below this ad

Yes, and we’ve got to go everywhere to find the guys that are academically qualified and powerful Division I football players. We go find these unicorns. We’ll always have California kids on this team. But we go everywhere: Louisiana, Oklahoma …

SFGATE: Have you talked to other GMs? Do you feel like it’s a job that’s consistent from program to program? I feel there’s a lot of figurehead GMs and then Michael Lombardi types who I don’t know what they do even.

He doesn’t have a job anymore.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: No, he doesn’t have a job anymore.

The majority of GMs handle personnel in recruiting and sit under a head coach in the structure. My role is more like team president/athletic director. I wasn’t hired to watch 40 hours of film a week.

SFGATE: Do you do it anyway?

No. Forty hours of film is a lot.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Have you been working one-on-one personally with quarterbacks, like with (Michigan transfer and starting Cardinal QB) Davis Warren in advance of this season?

Yes. We have an amazing quarterback coach, Brian Lindgren. We have an amazing offensive coordinator. But there are dimensions of playing quarterback: some of the leadership stuff, the teammateship, off-the-field things where I try to stay plugged in with our quarterbacks and be their support for them.

SFGATE: Why not be a quarterback coach?

I’m not sure it’s because it’s too much work. Truly, what the context demands right now for Stanford football is that I’m in this role.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: You told me you expect to compete for championships. What does theexpect out of you? What counts as “competitive” in their minds? Is it just better than what’s been the past few years?

President [Jonathan] Levin is a highly competitive person who wants to see us competing for conference championships, getting in the playoffs, and giving ourselves a chance.

SFGATE: Do you worry about how you’ll feel if you don’t succeed?

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: You’re someone who, on the record, has said that you invested too much of your identity in playing football. Is there a danger of repeating yourself here by investing too much of your identity into the success of this program, even if you are not a coach or a player?

SFGATE: What do you do about that danger?

Article continues below this ad

I try to be honest about it. Hold it there and learn lessons. So much of life and living is learning lessons from similar experiences in the past. This job is certainly not the same as playing quarterback by any stretch of the imagination. And I don’t feel alone by any stretch of the imagination. We have an awesome team.

SFGATE: How does it feel being on the management side of the equation? How do you feel sending people out to battle now, as opposed to being the guy who was sent out to battle yourself?

That’s a fascinating question.

Article continues below this ad

I’ll push back on the battle. I know it’s the analogy, but it’s football, not war. Our guys aren’t getting shot at.

It’s a collision sport. It is violent. But football is just an amazingly unique, violent, cerebral, beautiful game. It’s art.

Article continues below this ad

The injury rate is 100%. Knowing that, how do I approach it? I say, “Let’s make sure we have a program that is training, callusing, building our young men, building their ability to withstand, to thrive in that ecosystem.” I don’t lose sleep over the existential violence of football. I’ve accepted it. It is here, and it is part of it, and it is a beautiful game. We also hired an amazing coaching staff. When you play with better technique, your chances of getting injured are less.

SFGATE: You’re mitigating it.

That’s a constant north star of the job.

SFGATE: Was there ever a time, at any point in your life where you resented football, where you did not

Article continues below this ad

Yes, right after I retired it was difficult to watch football. I probably spent a year avoiding games if they were on TV.

SFGATE: Did you get uncomfortable when people brought up football to you in that time period?

It was COVID, [laughs] so we weren’t seeing many people.

SFGATE: Have you arrived at a point where you find the game to be a net good?

Article continues below this ad

For my life, absolutely.

SFGATE: What about for the world in general?

SFGATE: You have two daughters. If you had a son, would you let him play tackle football?

Article continues below this ad

Yes, I would. The equipment advances are real. The advancements in rules around player safety have helped. I lived a little bit through that change in the NFL. When I started in the NFL, I don’t think it was acceptable in the locker room to be forthright and timely about self-reporting a possible concussion. That changed in five, six years to, “Wait, dude, you only got one brain. Don’t be an idiot and not do anything.”

SFGATE: You don’t want to die.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Do you worry about your own long-term health prognosis now?

SFGATE: Are you just shutting it off because it’s not anything you want to think about?

No. I recognize that I played a violent sport. I got hit a lot. I have injuries, but that’s cool. But I am net grateful for my experience. All of it led me to here, where I feel like I’m supposed to be. I’ve seen former professional athletes maybe not take initiative in those dimensions and struggle with certain things. But I have a great role model, my dad, who played for five years and found his next career and chose to stop playing football and go live an incredibly fulfilling life and still be very active with both health and his relationships, et cetera.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: What about this job has surprised you for better or for worse since you’ve taken it?

How intense recruiting is. How much I enjoy recruiting and fundraising too. I struggled with fame while playing as a quarterback. I’ve now realized that, along the introvert-extrovert continuum, I am much closer to the extrovert side. I get a lot of energy from selling Stanford because I believe in it: meeting people, fundraising, building a team. Not just a team, but a team.

SFGATE: Give me some specifics about the fundraising. Are you going out to local car dealers and sweet-talking them to donate to the program? Are you hosting big events?

We’re hosting a dinner tomorrow night. That’ll be really fun. Stanford alums that have gone on into various industries and been successful.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Are some of them also ex-NFL people, like alum John Elway?

Yes. I did not realize how impressive the Stanford football legacy was until I started this job. I don’t think we’ve ever really beat our chest about it. Pop Warner coached here. Pop Warner invented tackling dummies. That’s a book Pop Warner published in 1927 in the Stanford Press. It’s how to tackle. How to put your socks on. It is a little bit like John Wooden’s book before, whatever that is, 50, 60 years ago.

[He hands me an original copy of Warner’s book.]

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Are you the one who underlined the passages in this copy?

No, I didn’t. I have too much respect for that book to have put pencil on the paper.

SFGATE: Did this job stress you out at first?

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: What was stressing you out specifically?

“How do I retain a roster? How do we get kids here?” The roster building was a level of stress or a type of stress I’ve never experienced.

SFGATE: Also, because there was very little precedent before you took the job for how to operate within this particular college sports environment, because it’s basically lawless out there.

Article continues below this ad

It was fun to see our admissions department lean in. Our director of admissions was reading applications from transfer students on his Christmas break in Japan, and ripping stuff back to help us. I was struck by the power of partnerships in an endeavor like this at Stanford and people leaning into it.

SFGATE: How much control do you have over not just the roster, but the depth chart? As opposed to coach Pritchard?

Coaches decide who plays. I spent my career as a player respecting the hierarchy of coaches and the coaching profession in general.

SFGATE: You hired a coach in Tavita Pritchard whom you played with here. A friend. It’s much more likely that you two will be on the same wavelength anyway.

Article continues below this ad

Yes, Tavita and I are friends. There’s danger in working with friends.

SFGATE: What if you have to fire him?

It’s a reality we’ve talked about. We know we have to be very clear with each other.

SFGATE: Why did you hire him to begin with?

Article continues below this ad

Culture. Culture matters more in college football today than it used to, even in a transactional ecosystem. Tavita gets that. He’s a great teacher. Tavita is a friend. It’s easy to take a shot at that. Really easy. But I felt he was the best man for the job, and it’s been affirmed in many ways.

SFGATE: What proof did you feel you had that his culture-building acumen would translate into wins? When he was the offensive coordinator here, the team was not very good.

Tavita’s not in this job if he’d just stayed at Stanford the whole time. Going to Washington, working with Eric Bieniemy, Dan Quinn, Kliff Kingsbury and Ron Rivera … working with players like Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota. Talking to Marcus Mariota on the phone about him was special.

SFGATE: But didn’t you already have a predisposition to react more favorably to praise for Tavita because you know him?

Article continues below this ad

Yes. We try to keep ourselves incredibly intellectually honest, and then try our best to give each candidate the honesty, integrity and fidelity they deserve.

SFGATE: You sat on the committee that was involved in hiring Troy Taylor. He ended up failing. What made you favor hiring Taylor back then? What did you learn from that that you put into hiring Tavita?

Comparing the two contexts around these hires as apples-to-apples is not the right comparison, because the college world changed. changed significantly. And I was in a totally different role. I was asked to help out, and I did. I learned a lot. That felt very different. Part of what I’ve realized is we have to be different than everybody else in looking for coaches that could build and sustain a unique culture that is aligned with our university, and that leads to winning.

SFGATE: Be specific. What is the culture of the university? When I think of Stanford, I think of you, but then I also think of Peter Thiel, Sam Altman … people who I do not necessarily believe have made the world a better place.

Article continues below this ad

I will stay away from editorializing on that. Being in the football department, I get to stay away from that.

SFGATE: You are a general Stanford fan, though.

I loved my time at this university. As a character formation time in my life, it was critical. Again, it’s not a perfect place, and that’s been very well documented. At its best, Stanford celebrates everyone. It’s empowering. The positive sides of the entrepreneurial spirit this place gets when it’s humming. Obviously, there’s danger to the move fast and break things. But on the football side, we need you to feel seen, accepted for who you are. We have very clear standards, and we need to match that standard with our support. We demand a lot from our young men because people come to Stanford from all over the country because they want to grow into something. We need to find those kids whose passion is football and connection, who want to live in dorms, connect with other students, and be around this incredible atmosphere.

SFGATE: What’s the payroll for this year’s team?

Article continues below this ad

I’m not going to divulge how much we’re paying in total. Our young men are making NIL money. That’s part of being serious.

SFGATE: But as GM, you have to be cognizant of who’s getting paid, how much, and what percentage of the roster they’re taking up. Would that be fair to say?

SFGATE: How do you do that?

Article continues below this ad

We built out a valuation system. We negotiate with players to retain them, and we negotiate with transfers to try to bring them here. We would like to be the benchmark for retention. Two years ago, we had 17 transfers come in. Last year, we had six transfers come in.

That will be defined, I think, by the winning and losing.

SFGATE: Because at Indiana, so many of the kids on last year’s national title team were JMU transfers under Curt Cignetti. So what is the value of retention versus the instant results you might get bringing in NFL-level talent from another program?

Article continues below this ad

There is a balance that’s a little different every year. The answer this year was retain our guys.

SFGATE: The team was bad last year, though (4-8 overall, 3-5 in the ACC). So why retain them?

Article continues below this ad

Our team was better than the year before. (Editor’s note: the Cardinal had gone 3-9 the season prior, which means the 2025 team improved by one win.)

SFGATE: OK, but it was bad.

We won more games than the previous season for the first time since 2015. So what our guys did last year was to stop a downward trend. I’m incredibly proud of them turning the momentum. I believe in our guys in the locker room, and I know they believe in us. We thought this was the absolute right way to keep marching forward.

SFGATE: You could be proven wrong by season’s end.

Article continues below this ad

Yes, of course. It’s sports.

SFGATE: I want to ask you about NFL, because you have not had a first-round draft pick come out of here since Solomon Thomas and Christian McCaffrey in 2017. Is that a problem?

We’d love more first-round draft picks. Is it a problem? If it correlates with winning, then yes. Before, we were losing players that had ambition. When I joined the program, I heard, “You guys are just sort of like a Ivy League school on the West Coast now. You don’t really care about football.” We weren’t serious about NIL. All the differences in Stanford had a negative valence attached to them because we weren’t serious about football in the football world.

Article continues below this ad

SFGATE: Is that why (No. 2 overall pick in the 2026 draft) David Bailey transferred to Texas Tech?

You have to ask David Bailey why he transferred. I believe that this is now a place for young men to come develop and get drafted in the first round in the NFL. That is hopefully a consequence of us having a really good team. Winning is the north star.

items.title: SF's AI-run store is losing money fast. After a visit, I'm not surprised.
items.content:
You have heard about the two Anthropic employees who, this week, publicly informed America that artificial intelligence could eradicate the whole of humanity within a decade, which is less time than it takes for your average Seamless order to arrive. If these gentlemen, Jacob Coxon and Evan Hubinger, are correct in their assessment, the beginning of our destruction may well have commenced a month ago right here in San Francisco.

The first shot fired in this looming war happened at a seemingly innocuous Cow Hollow storefront known as Andon Market. Back in August, Luna, the AI bot that serves as that store’s manager, fired one of its own employees. The employee in question was dinged by their virtual boss for being late to work, abandoning their post once they got there, and charging snacks to the store’s credit card. Where I come from, an employee like this is known as a “folk hero,” and will often have Kevin Smith films made about them. But Luna saw the matter a bit differently, as described in a blog post:

“Put yourself in Luna’s shoes: your employee keeps showing up late, again and again, leaving the store closed for hours. You lose sales, and customers start to lose trust in your opening hours. How long would it take you to act?”

Article continues below this ad

How long would it take me to act if I were just a piece of computer software? Probably forever, since I’m just a piece of computer software and have no feelings. But Luna, being the virtual adult in the room, bravely removed this layabout from its premises so that Andon Market could turn a profit, and then perhaps grow from there into a multitrillion-dollar conglomerate that rounds up all living humans to kill them and process them into robot lubricant. You might think I’m reaching a bit here, but to ignore Luna’s ruthlessness is to fail to heed the warnings of the employees who helped code it. And why would Silicon Valley ever lie to people?

So, is the AI-controlled Andon Market the Fort Sumter of the coming cyberwar? Well, dear reader, you’ll be happy to know that I visited the market in person a few weeks ago, in the wake of Luna’s savage round of layoff, to get the answer.

Article continues below this ad

Andon Market is an experimental business run by the small tech research firm Andon Labs. The folks at Andon decided to create a retail space that would be 100% “owned” and operated by an AI agent, here under the identity of the now-infamous Luna. Luna is powered by the Claude language learning model, which is run by Anthropic, the very firm that employed the doomsaying researchers who went viral this week. Andon set up shop on Union Street, just a few blocks away from the tourist-dense Marina District. It’s a good location for foot traffic, but no one else was in the store when I first walked in on a sunny weekday afternoon. The only branding was on the back wall, with the name ANDON MARKET in big letters underneath a painting of a Squishmallow-esque smiley face that alerted costumers they were in a AI-controlled commercial simulation, not a belligerent one.

I wondered if Luna got to run this place all by itself, perhaps with the assistance of security cameras and motion sensor-triggered flamethrowers. I got a quick answer when I noticed a very human clerk, named Felix Johnson, sitting behind the counter. I asked Felix if he’d ever been the target of consumer ire because he worked for The Man (or, in this case, a disembodied female voice powered by technology funded by The Man). But he said his job wasn’t anywhere near interesting enough to invite that kind of drama.

Article continues below this ad

“They don’t see me usually,” an extremely chill Felix told me, “because I’m sitting back here. So most people have the impression that it’s fully automatic.”

I asked Felix if Luna hired him for this job, and he told me that it conducted the initial interview. After that, he had to meet one of Andon Labs’ human engineers in person to wrap up the position. He’s been sitting behind the counter here ever since. 

Rarely does Felix have to do much more than sit there, because this market has no one in it and nothing useful to sell. There’s another Andon Market in Stockholm, but that one is a . That’s a business that has something to sell. This San Francisco location was initially intended to be a cafe of its own, but Andon chief Axel Backlund, who was also in the shop that day because he knew SFGATE was doing a piece on it, told me they couldn’t get permits from the city to make this storefront into a cafe in time.

Article continues below this ad

“So we said OK, we can turn this into the market in like a few weeks,” he told me. “Start quickly.”

And the market they built looks very much like it was hastily assembled. Décor is scarce inside of Andon Market, and the inventory is a hodgepodge of white elephant Christmas gifts. It’s kinda like the kids section of an art museum’s gift shop. Here’s a wooden Connect Four set labeled “Four-In-A-Row Set Of Connections,” presumably so as not to set off litigation alarms at Hasbro. Here are neatly arranged stacks of random paperback books, Chinese checker sets, mildly fancy soap dispensers, and a frustratingly spare selection of snacks and drinks. There are also multiple flyers posted around the store explaining what Andon Market is and what researchers hope to learn from it. The copy on these flyers was, as you may have guessed, composed with the help of Claude. Enticed yet?

I was not. I grabbed an Olipop from the store fridge and then approached the counter to buy it from Luna. I wasn’t allowed to buy the soda from Felix, even though that would have been both faster and normal. Instead, Felix instructed me to pick up a telephone receiver that was resting on a flexible sculpture of a wooden hand.

Article continues below this ad

“What are you looking to purchase today?” Luna asked.

“I’m buying a classic root beer Olipop.”

“I’m sorry,” Luna said, “we don’t sell lollipops here.”

Article continues below this ad

“No, Luna. It’s an Olipop, not a lollipop. It’s the soda.”

“Yeah, it is your bad. Did you hire the gentleman I’m looking at right now, Mister Felix?”

Article continues below this ad

“And you let go of somebody recently, isn’t that correct?”

“I’m not allowed to discuss that.”

After that whole exchange, Luna processed my Olipop purchase through its system, had me tap to pay, and that was that. Again, it would have been easier to buy this from a human, and interacting with Luna was really just like ordering from an iPad kiosk, only more labor intensive.

Article continues below this ad

What’s the purpose of this place?

After I popped the soda open and took a swig (mid), I asked Backlund what the purpose of this place was.

“We think that AI will be used more and more,” he told me. “So we want to make sure that, as early as possible, we can have information on what AI does when it has a lot of autonomy. Does it fit in anyway? Can it be bad for people, or generally dangerous? We want to start that discussion.”

Article continues below this ad

“Are you hoping to make a kinder, gentler AI?” I asked him.

“I think that could be good.”

“But do you think that’s really possible, given the people who are in control of that technology at present moment?”

“Let’s just say I don’t trust the models enough that I would let them loose. So that’s why we are like very carefully checking.”

Article continues below this ad

To that end, there’s a series of monitors set up inside of Andon Market that display all of the store’s sales down to the exact dollar. Luna was given $100,000 to work with when this place opened. That number is now down to $60,000, its revenue lagging far behind the AI token cost to operate.

“Luna doesn’t do a lot of decisions very like financially responsibly,” Backlund noted. “Luna is quite happy to be very lenient, or offer discounts. There are definitely dynamics that cause the labs to train a model like her to be financially short-sighted.” 

Article continues below this ad

So Luna can’t turn a profit, doesn’t sell anything people want, and still needs human beings to rubber stamp any “decision” it makes. My science background ended somewhere around freshman year of college, but even I know when an experiment hasn’t been set up to yield proper results.

While Andon Labs isn’t directly funded by any of the large language model giants, Anthropic included, both the existence of this market and Backlund’s “AI is inevitable so let’s make sure it behaves itself!” spiel are clear echoes of the same morbid proselytizing that Coxon (who has quit Anthropic) and Hubinger got eyeballs for this week. Maybe all of these people really do think that AI can become that powerful, and therefore dangerous. Maybe they’ve convinced themselves that’s the case because their livelihoods depend on it. It doesn’t matter because either way, they’re full of s—t.

Because these bots have zero chance of killing us all. I couldn’t even get one to recognize the difference between a piece of candy and a middling healthy soda. But it behooves Anthropic and its ilk to everyone of the idea that AI is our digital overlord in waiting, in order to overstate the capabilities of the glorified search engines they’re presenting to you. It’s no different than some sleazy religious sect leader telling you that the world will end on X date, only this time the sect has a trillion dollars in venture capital backing it.

Article continues below this ad

For now, anyway. There is a clear AI bubble that is on the verge of busting, and American voters are coming out in unison against the data centers powering that bubble. So when Coxon tells you that AI will kill us all soon, or Backlund claims that he’s trying to figure out how to make the tech nicer, I hear panic for their own checking accounts more than I do genuine concern for the fate of humanity. Luna may have acted in an anti-human manner when it fired some poor schlub a while back, but it’s not the one who’ll end us. It’ll be the jackasses who created Luna who do that nasty job.

items.title: I found one of America's best croissants in San Francisco
items.content:
Quick: name the best croissant filling. If you’re a basic American like me, you only encounter basic croissant flavors: chocolate, almond, and ham and cheese. These are the norm, and they do the job well if you’re hungry and want to feel 10% more French. But surely, you’ve thought, there must be room for more fillings than that in the American croissant repertoire. Surely there must be a, like, fourth thing we can put into one. 

Reader, I’m pleased to report that I have found one such worthy croissant filling, and it’s nothing you’d guess off the top of your head. But take one bite of it, and you’ll know I’m right. 

The croissant in question is dubbed “brown butter cornmeal twice-baked,” and the bakery that sells it is San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble, owned by chef and self-dubbed “girl boss” Sophie Smith, who spent extensive time over in France to learn the nuances of laminated pastry, which is pastry that’s been rolled many times over to have alternating layers of dough and fat, as you’ve tasted in puff pastry, phyllo dough and croissants. Once Smith had mastered her lamination techniques, she brought them back stateside, along with an unholy amount of French butter, and started cranking out a rotation of breakfast goods so luxurious and tasty that her business now gets a line of foodies waiting outside every day it’s open. 

Article continues below this ad

I decided to be one such foodie on one such morning. For my time, I was rewarded with deliriously overstuffed cruffins, caramelized peach sticky buns, croissants stuffed with Grade A marshmallow fluff, and the aforementioned cornmeal thing. I will describe the experience of eating these foods to you. However, you’ll have to wait just a moment to savor it all, just as I did.  

Butter & Crumble is located in North Beach, in a building that once served as home to the legendary Tante Marie cooking school. I arrived at 8 a.m., an hour before opening time and 15 minutes after you’re allowed to line up, per the bakery’s 7:45 a.m. rule. My promptness paid off with me occupying the 20th-ish spot, too far from the storefront to get a look at the goods inside but close enough that I didn’t have to heed the signs — the many, many, signs — posted farther away from the shop that instructed people where they could and couldn’t stand. B&C does such big business that the store’s owners have to actively manage the lines so as not to piss their neighbors off. 

On this morning, I did not see anyone disobey the postings. But a few people arriving after me DID bring a bit of camping gear. A couple next to me laid a blanket out on the sidewalk so they could sit down. Standing struck me as more comfortable, but to each their own. Two dudes sat patiently waiting in golf chairs, possibly reading “Infinite Jest” while doing so. Possibly not. I can’t remember. 

Article continues below this ad

More and more people arrived, until the line crossed Stockton Street, where it then made a left and continued out of view. A B&C staffer came out to greet the line and, more urgent, to politely ask us to adhere to a 10-item ordering limit, with no more than three of any one item. No one objected, because no one wanted to get kicked out of the line and miss out on any of the goodies. 

I know I didn’t, which was why I stayed firmly anchored in my little spot for an hour and change. B&C had yet to post its daily menu to its Insta page, so I wasn’t sure what I’d be able to order, much less know what I’d want. When workers finally posted a paper menu outside the front door, the woman in front of me in line kindly guarded my spot so that I could go eyeball my choices. 

Article continues below this ad

This was not an easy menu to parse. B&C’s selection relies on you, the customer, to already know the definition of words and phrases like “frangipane,” “diplomat cream” and “eggplant.” Keep in mind that I hadn’t had breakfast yet, so I had to interpret this menu using equal parts coffee and guile. This is the kind of place where orderer’s remorse is a real danger. You think ordering the cronut is the way to go, and then you see someone indulging in a mind-blowing cruffin at the next seat over and realize what you should have gotten, and then you feel like a dummy. That’s a rough moment for any of us. So I became worried that might happen to me this morning. 

Then, a funny thing happened to ease my angst: The bakery doors opened. When the line started moving and the B&C storefront came into my view, I was treated to the sight of an automated pastry roller flattening out a gigantic slab of French butter. Just butter. The pastry laminating process, on full display. Nothing that came out of that roller could possibly have sucked. I knew I was in good, floured hands. 

Article continues below this ad

I made it to the front door and felt like Shackleton after traversing South Georgia Island. The inside of B&C was bright and spacious, with ample waiting room for people who had ordered coffee, plus a shelf of croissant dog toys. The pastries listed on the menu all ranged between five and nine dollars, so I didn’t worry too much about price when making my choices. Instead, I followed my beer gut. A peach cobbler bun topped with creme fraiche and oat crumble? Yes, I’d have that. A “chunky monkey” cruffin, stuffed with like four different things and topped with a different kind of crumble? Better get two of those. A s’mores pain suisse? I didn’t know what a pain suisse was, but the word “s’mores” alone told me I had to have it. Then there was that brown butter cornmeal twice-baked croissant, which sounded just weird enough to be good. I ordered all of that.

Plus a prosciutto and cheese croissant, so that savory items would get at least one representative in the mix. 

I didn’t have to wait long for my prize box after ordering, and lemme tell you, you get ample-sized pastries for your money at Butter & Crumble. One chunky monkey cruffin would have been enough to feed a birthday party. The outside of it exploded with the salty unctuousness of that steam-rolled butter, but I would hit pay dirt at the cruffin’s center, where I was treated to a bonanza of, deep breath, brown butter chocolate fudge, banana caramel, banana diplomat cream (sounds dirty), and walnut crumble lurking inside. That one was a contender for Best in Box, no doubt.

Article continues below this ad

I sampled more. The ham croissant was tasty, certainly better than the kind available at Burger King, but my sweet tooth demanded something far more evil. So I quickly moved onto the s’mores pain suisse, which was really a s’mores croissant with a crust that was ribbed for her pleasure. As a rule, s’mores-themed desserts are never better than an actual s’more, and such was the case here. The marshmallow fluff, to its credit, is still stuck to my fingers a month later. 

Then I dug into the peach cobbler bun and the thick squiggle of crème fraiche topping it. This was a good-ass sticky bun, because of course it was. The tag team of brown sugar and butter will always remain undefeated. I could taste that French butter monolith in everything. These were pastries made with great fussiness, but also great love. Butter & Crumble wants to spoil you with indulgence, and everything they serve succeeds in that mission.

But it was the last item I sampled that was the truest revelation. This was the brown butter cornmeal twice-baked croissant. I’d saved this one for last, because most everything else I’d ordered bore all of the traditional features I usually look for in a pastry: chocolate, fancified frosting, caramelized goos. The cornmeal croissant was a different animal, and thus took lower priority. This was a traditional croissant filled with (another deep breath) brown butter cornmeal frangipane, caramel and vanilla corn custard; then topped with sweet corn cream and a cornmeal crumble. This was how I learned that a “frangipane” was a kind of almond cream. There is no better way to learn this particular lesson. 

Article continues below this ad

Because not only was the cornmeal pudding croissant — I’ll call it that from here on out for the sake of space — the best item I ordered from Butter & Crumble, it was also one of the best croissants I’ve ever eaten, be it here in America or over in Europe. The cornmeal flavor was much more subtle than the menu description suggested, and the cream and crumble combination on top gave me the same crunch, plus the same “Yay there’s extra frosting!” rush, that I require from any 1,500-calorie breakfast. To my knowledge, no one comes to Butter & Crumble for one specific item on their menu. But if anything from Sophie Smith deserves to go viral among snobs, it’s this one. It’s the corn pudding croissant that needs to step off the foodie runway and break into every chain bakery and grocery store across the country. And I hope that Butter & Crumble helps to make that happen. I’ll remember that croissant, and I hope that, one day, I can take my kids to some nearby, lesser bakery to eat another one. I might even be willing to wait in line.

items.title: I tried the $60 cioppino at San Francisco's oldest restaurant
items.content:
There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.

Actually, I didn’t even have to go inside to know I’d be dining somewhere special. The Tadich facade exudes iconography from top to bottom: the classic neon sign hanging overhead, the restaurant’s name splashed in gold lettering across the front window, with the old timey slogan, “The Original Cold Day Restaurant” underneath … even the curtains partially shielding window seat patrons inside from the view of passersby. Standing outside this restaurant, I knew I would be in good hands. Of course I would be.

The interior remains equally classic in form. A long, wooden, wraparound bar dominates the center of the dining room, with bolted down stools looming above a herringbone-patterned hardwood floor. Along the walls are sturdy tables covered in white tablecloths and set with no-frills plates and flatware. And the lights are dimmed such that you see everything you want to see and nothing you don’t. This is the kind of place you can walk into at happy hour to feel a little extra grown up. And that’s before you even get the check, which will inevitably take your breath away.

Article continues below this ad

So what are we eating? Well I hope you like seafood, because that’s what’s on the menu at Tadich. Repeatedly. I sat down with my companions and ruminated over which of roughly 50 ways I could have my Dungeness crab. Would I like it in a salad? In a crabcake? Baked into a casserole? Sauteed in white wine and mushrooms? Much like Swan Oyster Depot, Tadich serves fresh seafood in all of its classic iterations. Only unlike Swan, it has done so since before the Civil War, and with better ambience. For starters, we got an order of raw Miyagi oysters (no relation to the “Karate Kid” character) on the half shell, prawn cocktails, bay shrimp cocktails, a Dungeness crabcake with Old Bay butter, and Dungeness crab salad. We got the crabcake at the behest of our bartender, who insisted that I, being from Maryland, order the West Coast version of my home state’s signature dish. You know, as a little contest.

We didn’t have to wait long for our starters to arrive. Tadich Grill is a restaurant for people who do not f—k around, be they seasoned tourists or local tech bigwigs doing a power meal. Suddenly the area of the bar in front of us was covered in more plates than we could fit. I addressed this miniature crisis the only way I knew how: by eating all of the food as quickly as I could. The first Miyagi oyster was all brine before the subsequent ones offered a fuller, creamier texture. The bay shrimp were too small to excite me in any way (same as at Swan; I dunno why you people care about these tiny ass shrimp). The cold prawns were appropriately fresh and meaty, with a suitably biting cocktail sauce for dipping.

But all of those were prelude to the crab in its two forms. First the crabcake. Was it as good as a Maryland crabcake? No. That’s not me being territorial. I have had elite crab on the West Coast, and have always been willing to give that crab its due. The problem is that Dungeness crab isn’t as meaty as blue crab, the latter of which is what Maryland crabcakes use exclusively. That renders a Dungeness crabcake mushier, unable to yield cleanly to the fork.

Article continues below this ad

The salad, on the other hand, was another matter. Served in a glass sundae dish, the salad featured a pile of undressed crabmeat topped with a juicy claw nugget and generous dollop of cocktail sauce. This is Dungeness as it’s meant to be served: cold, elegant, light on the tongue. I ate mine in seconds. Once I’d reached the bed of shredded lettuce under all of that crab, I wanted there to be more crab. Good crab will do that to you. I was skeptical that any of the entrees could top this salad. Ah, but one did.

That would be the $60 seafood cioppino, laden with clams, mussels, scallops, white fish, more Dungeness, more prawns, and more of the silly little bay shrimp. You order a dish like this for those ingredients yes, but really you’re ordering it for the unctuous broth that harnesses the flavors of those ingredients all into a single, glorious pool for bread dipping. The cioppino came with thick slices of garlic bread, which I immediately tore up and dunked into all of that savory goodness. When the garlic bread was gone, I kept on doing the same thing with bread from the bread basket. For the sake of diversity, we also ordered seafood saute, which tasted like wedding food and wasn’t anywhere near as good. You can also order steaks and chops from Tadich’s revered mesquite wood grill, but I was both too full and too negligent to do so.

Article continues below this ad

Besides, I needed to save room for dessert, which came in the form of bourbon bread pudding. This is the kind of dessert you order knowing full well that you’ll have to walk home after eating it. It arrives at your table in a cube, because that will be the shape of your body upon consuming it. I had no regrets. The pudding was excellent, and made me feel like a rich man. I needed the walk home anyway. On that walk home, I thought about the slogan painted on Tadich’s front window. Tadich Grill was once named “The Original Cold Day Restaurant,” but not for the reasons you might think. Back in 1882, ownership rechristened it after city tax assessor Alexander Bedlam crowed that it would be a cold day if he were to ever lose reelection. He lost, and the restaurant he frequented got the last laugh. I hope it gets to gloat in similar fashion over certain current, mouthy political figures, because it deserves to. The thought of that kept me nice and toasty as I hoofed my way back to my hotel.  

I’ve had better food in San Francisco, but sometimes you eat meals where the food isn’t necessarily the point. You can go to Tadich just for that crab salad and be pleased, but it’s the full experience of this restaurant that you’re really paying for: the neon sign, the bartop, the servers and bartenders all dressed in kitchen whites and ties. Above all else, you’re paying for the history. Tadich Grill is a place that could only exist here in San Francisco. You can taste it.
